title: Household Consumption Expenditure Survey: 2022-23 & 2023-24: Nutritional Intake in India
authors: Government of India Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation; National Statistics Office
access: Table 1 on printed p. 2 labels 61.8/63.4 as per-capita-per-day 2023-24 protein. Table 3 on printed p. 7 places the same 61.8/63.4 under unadjusted, with adjusted 2023-24 protein at 61.2 rural and 62.9 urban. Rendered printed p. 5 confirms Figure 5R 2023-24 rural cereals 45.9 and egg/fish/meat 12.4; Figure 5U 2023-24 urban cereals 38.7 and egg/fish/meat 14.1.
findings: HCES collection periods were August 2022-July 2023 and August 2023-July 2024.
All-India unadjusted per-capita protein intake was 61.9 g/day rural and 63.2 g/day urban in 2022-23; 61.8 g/day rural and 63.4 g/day urban in 2023-24.
In 2023-24, egg/fish/meat contributed 12.4% of rural protein intake and 14.1% of urban protein intake; cereals contributed 45.9% rural and 38.7% urban.
Adjusted per-capita protein intake in 2023-24 was 61.2 g/day rural and 62.9 g/day urban.
limitations: Nutrient estimates are generated from household food-consumption data and nutrient-content values, not individual dietary recalls. Household consumption accounting required adjustment for meals served to non-household members and purchased cooked meals.
funding: Government of India official statistics release; no conflict statement in press note.
excerpt: estimates of per day per capita and per day per consumer unit intake
use_in_synthesis: Use for official grams/day protein estimates and food-group contribution to protein, while distinguishing from self-reported frequency and market behavior.

title: National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India: Volume I
authors: International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS); ICF
access: The IIPS landing page was readable and links to rchiips.org. Direct rchiips HTTPS fetch returned 404 in this environment; DHS mirror PDF was downloaded and text-extracted. Table 10.25 on printed p. 437 explicitly covers women and men age 15-49. It reports women n=724,115 and men n=93,144. Women Fish, chicken or meat is 5.9 daily plus 39.3 weekly in Table 10.25, while Table 10.26.1 total at least once a week is 45.1; use the report's tabulated 45.1 for at-least-weekly claims. Men Fish, chicken or meat is 8.0 daily plus 49.3 weekly = 57.3 and Table 10.26.2 total age 15-49 also reports 57.3. Religion rows are on printed p. 438.
sample: The report says NFHS asked how often respondents consume various food types with response options daily, weekly, occasionally, or never.
findings: NFHS-5 gathered information from 636,699 households, 724,115 women, and 101,839 men.
Fieldwork occurred in two phases from 17 June 2019 to 30 January 2020 and from 2 January 2020 to 30 April 2021.
Table 10.25 reports women and men age 15-49 by frequency of consuming foods: daily, weekly, occasionally, or never.
For women age 15-49, weekly/daily consumption was 45.1% eggs, 35.7% fish, 35.9% chicken/meat, and 45.1% fish/chicken/meat.
For men age 15-49, weekly/daily consumption was 57.8% eggs, 45.8% fish, 46.9% chicken/meat, and 57.3% fish/chicken/meat.
Among women age 15-49 consuming fish/chicken/meat at least weekly, Table 10.26.1 reports 40.7% Hindu, 70.2% Muslim, 78.0% Christian, 7.9% Sikh, 62.2% Buddhist/Neo-Buddhist, and 4.3% Jain.
Among women age 15-49 consuming fish/chicken/meat at least weekly, Table 10.26.1 reports 47.7% Scheduled caste, 46.0% Scheduled tribe, 42.0% OBC, and 47.7% Other.
limitations: Self-reported frequency only; no portion size, grams, calories, purchase, price, outlet, or brand. Do not infer robust vegetarian identity or national vegetarian prevalence from the fish/chicken/meat frequency proxy. Men's individual survey response-rate section covers eligible men age 15-54, but cited food-consumption tables are explicitly women and men age 15-49.
funding: Funding by Government of India / MoHFW; technical assistance by ICF through the USAID-funded DHS Program; ICMR/NARI support for DBS component.
use_in_synthesis: Use to show heterogeneity in animal-source-food frequency by sex, religion, caste/tribe, residence, and wealth; do not use as volume or adoption evidence.
publication_date_note: Report volume says March 2022; suggested citation lists 2021.

title: Food balances (Global, National - 2010-2023 - Annual) - FAOSTAT
authors: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
locations_checked: FAO API rows for India 2023 item codes 2901, 2903, 2941
findings: India 2023 Grand Total protein supply in FAOSTAT food balances: 74.57 g/capita/day.
India 2023 Vegetal Products protein supply: 54.56 g/capita/day.
India 2023 Animal Products protein supply: 20.01 g/capita/day.
Animal Products account for about 26.8% of FAOSTAT protein supply in 2023.
limitations: Food balances estimate supply available for human consumption, not actual individual intake. National averages hide distributional heterogeneity. Rows include estimated/imputed flags.
funding: FAO statistical database under CC-BY-4.0; no study conflict statement.
excerpt: per caput supply figures represent only the average supply
use_in_synthesis: Use only as a supply-side comparator and to prevent confusion between supply and intake.

title: A Survey of Consumer Perceptions of Plant-Based and Clean Meat in the USA, India, and China
authors: Christopher Bryant; Keri Szejda; Nishant Parekh; Varun Deshpande; Brian Tse
findings: Total sample n=3,030 with India n=1,024.
Samples were representative by age and gender quotas, but India and China were disproportionately urban, higher-income, and well-educated.
In India, 56.3% reported being very or extremely likely to purchase clean meat in the hypothetical measure; 10.7% were not at all likely.
In India, 62.8% reported being very or extremely likely to purchase plant-based meat; 5.5% were not at all likely.
India survey was distributed in English.
limitations: Stated intention, not buying, repeat buying, or displacement. Skewed online sample; not nationally representative beyond age/gender quotas. Authors warn about self-report, future-behavior prediction, and social-desirability bias.
funding: Funded by Animal Advocacy Research Fund; conflict statement notes author roles/ties with The Good Food Institute and cellular-agriculture advocacy.
excerpt: poor ability to predict one's own future behavior
use_in_synthesis: Use for early-consumer stated receptivity and predictors, not national adoption.

title: Is India Ready for Alt-Meat? Preferences and Willingness to Pay for Meat Alternatives
authors: Rashmit S. Arora; Daniel A. Brent; Edward C. Jaenicke
access: Direct MDPI HTML/PDF/XML requests returned access-denied pages in this environment; the web crawl exposed article sections and metadata. Crossref lists only the MDPI version-of-record PDF and no archive. Searches found Penn State Pure/RePEc/EconPapers metadata records but no primary author institutional full text. Treat as bounded citation: DOI/publisher citation is safe, but avoid unverified table-page claims.
locations_checked: Funding and conflict statements via publisher text/search cache
findings: Face-to-face survey in Mumbai in December 2018; 424 interviews conducted and final working sample n=394 after dropping incomplete responses.
Survey was bilingual English/Hindi.
Discrete-choice experiment compared conventional meat, plant-based meat, clean/cell-based meat, and chana/chickpeas.
Latent-class model identified four segments; Classes 3 and 4 collectively made up 51.6% of sample and showed strong positive preferences toward simulated meat versus chana.
The plant-based meat enthusiast class was the largest segment at 32%.
limitations: Mumbai-only sample; not nationally representative. Stated preference / willingness-to-pay experiment, not real purchase, adoption, or displacement. At study time, authors characterized India's plant-based meat market as small and cell-based meat market as nonexistent.
funding: Funded by Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences Competitive Grant Program and Department of International Agriculture Special Initiative Funds; authors declare no conflicts of interest.
excerpt: The plant-based meat market in India is small
use_in_synthesis: Use for segmentation and WTP heterogeneity, especially matched product/meal substitution, not for national market-size claims.

title: DBT-BIRAC Joint Call for Proposals on 'Smart Proteins' for Fostering High Performance Biomanufacturing under BioE3 Policy
authors: Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council; Department of Biotechnology
findings: Smart proteins are identified as a BioE3 thematic subsector.
DBT/BIRAC invited proposals for fermentation-derived, plant-based, and cell culture-based proteins.
The call includes TRL 3-5 discovery/application research and TRL 5-7 scale-up/pilot/pre-commercial support.
Announcement date was 22 February 2025; last submission date was extended to 5 April 2025.
limitations: Call for proposals is not evidence of product approval, consumer adoption, safety clearance, retail availability, or displacement. Needs pairing with later implementation source for status.
excerpt: Discovery and application oriented Integrated Network research
use_in_synthesis: Use as evidence of official R&D/translation commitment.

title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: IMPLEMENTATION OF BIOE3 POLICY
authors: Press Information Bureau; Ministry of Science & Technology
access: The full PIB body posted 23 July 2026 states that BioE3 sectors include Smart proteins and functional foods, and states under Smart Protein that 9 projects have been supported in fermentation-derived/single-cell, plant-based, and cell-culture-based smart proteins.
findings: Union Cabinet approved BioE3 in August 2024.
Six thematic sectors include Smart proteins and functional foods.
Across BioE3 verticals, 11 calls were announced, over 2,000 proposals received, and over 270 projects recommended for funding.
Under the Smart Protein sector, 9 projects were supported in fermentation-derived/single-cell proteins, plant-based smart proteins, and cell-culture-based smart proteins.
The release frames projects as product/technology development and pilot/pre-commercial biomanufacturing support.
limitations: Not a food-regulatory approval source. Not evidence of retail adoption, consumer buying, displacement, or market size. Does not list all smart-protein recipients or product statuses in the excerpt.
funding: Official Government of India PIB release reporting a written Rajya Sabha answer.
excerpt: 9 projects have been supported in three categories
use_in_synthesis: Use as the strongest current official status source for policy commitment and supported project scope.

title: Household Integrated Economic Survey (HIES) 2024-25
authors: Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, Ministry of Planning Development and Special Initiatives
locations_checked: Table 3.7.C on printed page 25 / PDF text layer @P41 / screenshot pageno 41
findings: Field period September 2024 to June 2025; report preface says 32,814 households covered across Pakistan including AJK and GB.

Monthly per capita selected quantities in 2024-25 total: wheat/wheat flour 6.59 kg; rice/rice flour 0.86 kg; pulses 0.26 kg; milk fresh & boiled 6.15 litres; mutton 0.05 kg; beef 0.11 kg; chicken 0.34 kg; eggs 2.83 numbers.
Urban/rural comparison for 2024-25: chicken 0.41 kg urban vs 0.29 kg rural; eggs 3.44 urban vs 2.44 rural; wheat/wheat flour 5.76 kg urban vs 7.12 kg rural.

Quintile food expenditure shares rise for mutton, beef, fish, fruit, and hotels/restaurants as consumption quintile increases; wheat and vegetable ghee shares fall.

authors: Pakistan Bureau of Statistics
findings: HIES 2024-25 was carried out through tablet-based enumeration during September 2024 to June 2025.

HIES provides national/provincial information with urban/rural breakdown and consumption quintiles.

title: Households food consumption pattern in Pakistan: Evidence from recent household integrated economic survey
authors: Naveed Hayat; Ghulam Mustafa; Bader Alhafi Alotaibi; Roshan K. Nayak; Muhammad Naeem
findings: Uses PBS HIES 2018-19 cross-sectional data.
Initial sample 24,809 households; final analytic data 24,620 households after missing records.
LA/AIDS model over eight food groups: cereals, pulses, milk, ghee, meat, fruits, vegetables, sugar.
Finds milk, meat, and fruits are luxury food items; cereals, pulses, vegetables, sugar, and ghee are necessity items.
All eight food groups have inelastic compensated own-price elasticities.
limitations: National-level model only, eight food groups only. Does not include consumer acceptance of alternative proteins. Underlying microdata not re-run in this task.
funding: Visible article note: 'The authors extend their appreciation to The Researchers Supporting Project number (RSP2023R443) King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.' PubMed conflict statement: authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships. Focused searches of PubMed, ScienceDirect, OpenAlex, DOAJ, and correction/retraction queries found no correction or retraction notice as of 2026-09-14.
excerpt: milk, meat, and fruits are luxuries food items

title: Attitudes and Perceptions Towards Cultured Meat Among General Population in Pakistan
authors: Muhammad Ahsan; Muhammad Uzair; Moazzam Ali
findings: Cross-sectional online survey in Pakistan, January-March 2021.
417 completed; 4 excluded; final n=413.
Sample: mean age 34, male 77.8%, meat eaters 75.3%, vegetarians 23.4%, vegans 1.2%.

Abstract/results text reports acceptance of cultured meat at 27.1%, but this should be caveated or omitted in polished prose because the item-level willingness totals are more specific and internally uneven.
Willing to eat cultured meat: strongly agree 23.5%, agree 4.1%, uncertain 21.6%, disagree 45.8%, strongly disagree 5.0%.
Willing to pay premium prices: strongly agree 9.9%, agree 2.2%, uncertain 28.9%, disagree 41.0%, strongly disagree 18.0%.
Religious norm item: 60.5% disagreed that CM production is not against religious norms.
limitations: Not nationally representative. Online/social-media sampling, young and male-heavy. No tasting; intention and perception only. PDF footer has placeholder DOI text, but journal metadata provides DOI. Recommended use: omit headline 27.1% acceptance percentage except in a caveated source note; use item-level willingness and barrier figures instead.
funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest.

title: Understanding Key Factors Influencing Consumers' Willingness to Try, Buy, and Pay a Price Premium for Mycoproteins
authors: David Dean et al.
findings: Mycoprotein is fungal-based and distinct from plant-based meat analogues and cultivated meat.
Survey administered in 2018/2019 in 12 countries including Pakistan.
Pakistan subsample in Table 1: n=649, male 65.6%, female 34.1%, mean age 23.6, omnivore 77.2%, flexitarian 15.3%, vegetarian 7.6%.
Pooled model R2: 0.316 willingness to try, 0.264 willingness to buy, 0.237 willingness to pay premium.
Pooled drivers: healthiness, nutritional benefits, safety, sustainability; affordability and taste mixed.
limitations: Pooled multinational model, not Pakistan-specific estimates. Online recruitment and stated willingness. Not precision-fermentation evidence for dairy/egg proteins.
excerpt: Affordability and taste had mixed results.

title: FAO analysis highlights strategic policy reform to narrow Pakistan's healthy diet gap
authors: FAO Agrifood Economics and Policy Division; FAO Food and Nutrition Division; FAO Pakistan Office; Aga Khan University partners
findings: Analysis compared current food supply gaps/surpluses against Pakistan National Food-Based Dietary Guidelines 2018.
FAO summary says vegetables, fruits, and pulses may be supply-constrained while cereals, sugar, and oils are available in excess relative to healthy diet needs.
Reducing food loss was described as most impactful and cost-effective, with an eight percent reduction in cost of healthy diets.
Scenario list included reducing losses, increasing deficit-sector productivity, and reallocating support from wheat to fruits/vegetables.
limitations: Event/news summary rather than full technical model. Should be used for policy context, not detailed quantitative modeling.
excerpt: not about producing more food, but producing the right food

title: Country Brief: Pakistan
authors: FAO Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS)
findings: 2025 cereal production estimated at 53 million tonnes, slightly above average.
Wheat flour prices surged by about 50-90% in most markets between July 2025 and January 2026, near-record levels.
About 10 million people estimated in IPC Phase 3 or above between April and July 2025.
Severe flooding in 2025 affected at least 5.8 million people.
limitations: Food security and price context, not protein consumption data. IPC estimates apply to acute food insecurity populations and periods.
excerpt: Wheat flour prices at near-record level.

title: Pakistan Halal Authority official pages
authors: Pakistan Halal Authority
findings: PHA says it was established under Ministry of Science and Technology through Act No. VIII of 2016.
PHA mandate includes ascertaining halal status of products, processes, and services in local markets and imports/exports.
Registered local HCB list includes multiple certification bodies and validity dates.
Licensed-products page includes dairy/dairy substitutes and gelatin examples but no reviewed entry for cultivated meat or precision-fermented dairy/egg proteins.

title: Most plant-based meat alternative buyers also buy meat: an analysis of household demographics, habit formation, and buying behavior among meat alternative buyers
authors: Zachary T. Neuhofer and Jayson L. Lusk
access: Full text XML retrieved and inspected
locations_checked: Methods, Data; Results, General household behavior; Discussion and conclusions
sample: 38,966 US households purchasing relevant meat or PBMA products, November 2018 to November 2020; ground products/patties/burgers
findings: Most PBMA purchasers also bought ground meat; a first PBMA purchase did not coincide with a fall in observed ground-meat buying in the before/after comparison.

title: Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
authors: Philipp Schoenegger, Indre Tuminauskaite, Peter S. Park, Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos, and Philip E. Tetlock
sample: 12 LLMs, 31 binary questions, 925 human tournament participants, October 2023 to January 2024
findings: An LLM aggregate beat a no-information benchmark and was statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd; the authors also identify poor calibration and a small question sample.
limitations: Does not validate long-run India–Pakistan protein-consumption forecasts, cultural simulation, or general equivalence to expert superforecasters.
funding: Forecasting Research Institute. Schoenegger disclosed being a Pro Forecaster at Metaculus.
